content: Inborn errors of metabolism are genetic disorders that result in abnormalities in the synthesis and metabolism of proteins, carbohydrates, or fats. In certain cases, it has been suggested that carnitine supplementation may be beneficial for infants suspected of having a metabolic disease, particularly as a temporary measure while awaiting diagnostic test results. Carnitine supplementation is a recognized treatment for primary carnitine deficiency and is also used when carnitine deficiency arises as a secondary complication in various inborn errors of metabolism, such as organic acidemias and fatty acid oxidation disorders, in both children and adults. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of carnitine supplementation in managing inborn errors of metabolism. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group's Inborn Errors of Metabolism Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, LILACS, and Iranmedex. The search also included reference lists of relevant articles. The most recent search of the Inborn Errors of Metabolism Register was performed on October 27, 2011. The review aimed to include randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared carnitine supplementation (administered in varying doses, frequencies, or durations) with placebo in children and adults diagnosed with inborn errors of metabolism. Two independent reviewers screened and assessed the eligibility of the identified trials. However, no trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. As a result, there is no high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials to support or refute the use of carnitine supplementation in the treatment of inborn errors of metabolism. This lack of evidence does not imply that carnitine is ineffective or should not be used in these conditions. Instead, clinicians are advised to rely on their clinical experience and consider the preferences of individual patients when making treatment decisions. Given the absence of robust evidence regarding the efficacy, safety, optimal dosage, and frequency of carnitine supplementation, current prescribing practices should be carefully observed and monitored. Further research is urgently needed, and future studies should adhere to the methodological standards outlined in the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement. Ethical considerations must also be taken into account, particularly when designing placebo-controlled trials for potentially life-threatening conditions such as carnitine transporter disorder or glutaric aciduria type I.
